segments.title: Why make battlecruisers a separate treaty category?
segments.body: A separate battlecruiser allowance changes the incentives facing every signatory. Britain could plausibly have made a distinct battlecruiser squadron a condition of participation, and the United States would have had reason to accommodate it to secure British and Japanese agreement. The allowance would have to sit alongside battleship tonnage, just as carrier tonnage did, because forcing the United States to trade away part of its fifteen-ship battle fleet would make agreement unlikely. The change would affect capital ships, carriers, cruiser limits, and each government's willingness to keep the treaty.

evidence.note: The transcript sets out the separate-category premise and the diplomatic rationale for it.

segments.summary: The alternate treaty begins by separating battlecruisers from battleships, a change intended to satisfy British and Japanese interests while preserving a workable agreement.

segments.title: Anglo-American competition without an expected war
segments.body: The interwar Anglo-American naval relationship was a friendly qualitative contest rather than a race toward war. British and American officers competed over technology, design quality, and national prestige while maintaining extensive professional and political contact. Politicians in both countries nevertheless wanted visible economies after the First World War. Cutting construction too sharply risked shipbuilding infrastructure, industrial competitiveness, and the ability to resume production later. Treaty restraint therefore carried the less visible cost of losing skilled yards and design continuity.

evidence.note: The transcript describes a friendly qualitative naval competition and warns that excessive economies damaged British and American industrial capacity.

segments.summary: British and American naval competition remained a friendly qualitative contest, but the political demand for a peace dividend risked damaging both countries' shipbuilding capacity.

segments.title: Treaty ratios through national strategic needs
segments.body: The American requirement for a fifteen-ship battle fleet is tied to keeping credible forces on two coasts. Britain faces a different distribution problem across home waters, the Mediterranean, and the Far East, while Japan's single-ocean focus is also its economic lifeline. France and Italy share a nominal ratio but have unequal strategic burdens, making the Mediterranean balance central to the treaty bargain. Britain benefits when Japan absorbs American attention and France and Italy balance one another, leaving the Royal Navy greater freedom elsewhere. The familiar 5:5:3:1.75:1.75 formula therefore reflects geography, alliance calculations, and the minimum force each government believed it could accept.

evidence.note: The 5:5:3 balance and the differing strategic demands on the treaty powers.

segments.summary: The familiar capital-ship ratios look different when viewed through American two-ocean planning, British imperial commitments, Japanese security, and the Franco-Italian Mediterranean balance.

segments.title: Why Anglo-American war plans did not make war likely
segments.body: The existence of Anglo-American war plans is weak evidence that conflict was imminent. Dense diplomatic, legislative, executive, naval, and royal contacts made an uncontrolled crisis highly unlikely under the existing governments. Armed forces still had a duty to plan against the strongest plausible opponent, however friendly that opponent might be. Such planning tested their ability to fight a peer and made lesser contingencies easier to understand. Staff preparedness should therefore be separated from political intent.

evidence.note: Why professional contingency planning should not be mistaken for an expectation of Anglo-American war.

segments.summary: Contingency plans for an Anglo-American war were professional planning exercises, not proof that either government expected the close relationship to collapse into conflict.

segments.title: Carrier limits in a battlecruiser treaty
segments.body: The historical carrier ceiling reflected the size and speed of ships likely to threaten or accompany carriers. At this early stage, flight operations still involved light aircraft, deck wires, and sailors physically helping to catch landing aircraft, so designers were not yet optimizing for the later demands of heavy air groups. In this alternate settlement, battlecruisers remain an active category, forcing carriers to keep pace with faster ships and survive pursuit by them. The carrier question therefore cannot be treated separately from the capital-ship settlement. Japanese construction choices could also determine whether Akagi becomes a carrier or remains a capital-ship project.

evidence.note: The transcript links carrier limits and conversions to a separate battlecruiser category.

segments.summary: Separating battlecruisers forces a rethink of carrier tonnage, speed, and the conversion of unfinished battlecruiser hulls.

segments.title: A 42,000-ton battlecruiser and 37,000-ton battleship limit
segments.body: Hood's displacement makes a distinct battlecruiser ceiling difficult: a seven-thousand-ton advantage over battleships would be too large, so the alternate scheme raises the battleship limit as well. American comparisons already treated Hood as equivalent to a Colorado-class battleship, which helps explain why that battlecruiser advantage would be difficult to accept. The resulting five-thousand-ton gap is paired with the same maximum sixteen-inch gun calibre and no artificial treaty speed limit. Raising the battleship ceiling from 35,000 to 37,000 tons also gives each power some additional aggregate tonnage without overturning the agreed ratios. A 32,000-ton carrier limit follows because carriers must operate alongside faster capital ships and need more machinery, range, and aviation capacity. Britain might nevertheless spread its 160,000-ton carrier allowance across more ships rather than build every hull to the individual maximum. These figures work as a linked package rather than as independent adjustments.

evidence.note: Revised limits for battlecruisers, battleships, and carriers.

segments.summary: The proposed treaty uses Hood to anchor a 42,000-ton battlecruiser ceiling, raises battleships to 37,000 tons, and expands the carrier allowance to 32,000 tons.

segments.title: Heavier cruisers reshape German commerce raiding
segments.body: The alternative treaty's changes ripple below the capital-ship level. A 12,000-ton cruiser armed with 9.2-inch guns becomes plausible because more battlecruisers would intensify concern about trade protection and economic warfare. Such a ship would be difficult to balance within the displacement limit, but it resembles an enlarged County-class answer to the increased raider threat. In this setting, cruisers with 9.2-inch guns would make an eleven-inch German raider a much less comfortable proposition. Combined with more fast capital ships, they could change the rationale for the Deutschland class and redirect later German naval development. That response would interact with the industrial damage and restrictions left by Versailles, so detailed predictions about the resulting Second World War become increasingly uncertain.

evidence.note: The transcript connects an enlarged cruiser limit to commerce protection and German design choices.

segments.summary: Allowing 12,000-ton, 9.2-inch cruisers gives British and American planners stronger commerce-war tools and makes German pocket-battleship ideas less attractive.

segments.title: Why France and Italy favour fast battleships
segments.body: For Italy, a battlecruiser cannot retain enough freedom of movement in the confined Mediterranean if rival ships can match its speed; armour therefore matters more. Speed still matters because it permits rapid redeployment between the basin's strategic points, but it must be combined with battle-line protection. The Francesco Caracciolo design consequently fits Italian needs better than a lightly protected cruiser-killer. France has a wider imperial rationale for battlecruisers, yet spending on them would weaken its position against Italy in the Mediterranean. The scenario accordingly pushes both navies toward fast battleships, while the French may have to abandon incomplete designs and start again.

evidence.note: Italian Mediterranean requirements contrasted with France's imperial and Mediterranean trade-offs.

segments.summary: Mediterranean geography makes speed and protection more useful to Italy and France than a separate battlecruiser force, even though France could use one for imperial duties.

segments.title: A treaty each power has reason to keep
segments.body: The revised arrangement separates battlecruiser tonnage while allowing France and Italy to combine their allocations into 265,000-ton capital-ship pools. Japan's separate battleship and battlecruiser allowances would total 459,000 tons. The proposal is political as well as arithmetic: arms-control systems endure when their participants see them as broadly serving their interests. An equitable settlement need not give every government everything it wants, but it must satisfy enough of each government's security, economy, and prestige goals. A ten-year restraint becomes more credible if disarmers obtain limits and navies still obtain forces they can regard as adequate. Treaty legitimacy therefore matters as much as nominal equality.

evidence.note: The transcript defines an equitable treaty as one that gives each party enough reason to preserve it.

segments.summary: The proposal aims for an equitable, not equal, settlement: each navy gives up something but retains enough security and building opportunity to support the treaty.

segments.title: Why Washington wanted Britain's older capital ships gone
segments.body: The disposal of Britain's older 13.5-inch-gun capital ships answered an American concern about how imperial naval strength might survive nominal limits. If those ships remained, Britain could modernize them late in the 1920s, pass some to the dominions, and then add a new Royal Navy programme on top. Washington therefore had reason to insist that the older hulls disappear rather than merely leave the active British list. That concession also helps explain why the United States was willing to permit new British ships under the treaty. Arms-control calculations counted usable imperial capability, not merely the headline tonnage of the core fleet.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the American fear that Britain's older 13.5-inch ships could be refitted, transferred to the dominions, and supplemented by new construction.

segments.summary: American negotiators feared Britain could refit its 13.5-inch-gun ships, transfer them to the dominions, and still build a new fleet, so scrapping the older ships helped make fresh British construction acceptable.

segments.title: A Royal Navy programme that sustains shipbuilding
segments.body: The proposal gives the Royal Navy an eight-ship, 37,000-ton battleship programme alongside up to three new large battlecruisers and its surviving ships. The battlecruisers could resemble F3 or G3 thinking, with sixteen-inch guns and enough protection to hunt enemy battlecruisers while Hood, Renown, and Repulse range more widely against commerce. Battleship orders in 1922, 1924, 1926, and 1928, with battlecruiser orders between them, would spread costs and allow lessons from each completed pair to shape the next design. The additional displacement could produce 28-knot battleships and encourage comparable machinery upgrades for the Queen Elizabeth class. Continuous orders would keep designers, skilled yards, and supporting industry active, making later refits and new construction less expensive than rebuilding capacity from scratch. The availability of new capital ships could also reduce pressure to turn cruiser construction into a substitute national-prestige race.

evidence.note: The transcript describes British force numbers, staggered orders, 28-knot battleships, and the industrial logic of continuity.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy could use separate tonnage pools to build eight fast battleships and several new battlecruisers in staggered orders that preserve design learning and yard capacity.

segments.title: Why continuous building makes later warships cheaper
segments.body: Restarting a dormant shipbuilding base costs far more than sustaining one that is already producing ships. A steady British capital-ship programme would preserve designers, skilled labour, supplier networks, and yard infrastructure into the 1930s. Orders could rotate through six yards, or concentrate battleship and battlecruiser work among fewer facilities while heavier cruiser construction supports others. That continuity would make major refits of Hood, Renown, and Repulse easier to schedule because newer ships could cover their absence. It would also reduce the temptation to load national prestige onto treaty-cruiser programmes. Force structure and industrial economics together determine whether later rearmament is affordable.

evidence.note: The transcript links continuous orders to refit availability, retained yards and skills, lower restart costs, and less cruiser prestige pressure.

segments.summary: A steady interwar order cycle keeps yards, skills, and supporting industries alive, reducing the cost of later refits and new construction.

segments.title: Japan's Kongo force and new battleship choices
segments.body: The separate category gives Japan enough battlecruiser tonnage to retain all four Kongos, with roughly 16,000 tons left for improvements. A 37,000-ton battleship category then opens a choice between reducing the Tosa design, adapting Kii ideas, or beginning an entirely new fast battleship. Four new ships would affect Japanese cruiser work and later capital-ship development, but they would not overturn the treaty ratio. These options give Japan visible scope for renewal and the prestige of continued construction. That sense of naval security matters politically because states that feel less threatened are less likely to interpret every rival move as existential.

evidence.note: The transcript examines Kongo tonnage, four possible new Japanese battleships, and the security implications.

segments.summary: Japan could retain all four Kongos within a separate battlecruiser allowance while gaining room for four new battleships, changing both force planning and perceptions of security.

segments.title: French redesign versus an Italian Caracciolo programme
segments.body: The French choices are presented as difficult: their best response may be to pause, abandon the Normandie and perhaps the Lyon-class direction, and invest in infrastructure rather than rush a poor design. Later Dunkerque- and Richelieu-class work demonstrates that France could produce excellent ships once it developed a suitable answer. Italy, by contrast, could use its allowance to complete four Francesco Caracciolo-class hulls and later add four new vessels. Finishing ships for which material had already been purchased would preserve employment and industrial capability more effectively than scrapping them. If a Caracciolo reached service first, it could become the reference point for the fast-battleship era and push Britain toward 28-knot successors. A 28-knot Italian battle line would also pressure the Royal Navy to avoid slow new designs, while standardizing on fifteen-inch guns could simplify Italian logistics.

evidence.note: The transcript compares French design decisions with the Italian case for completing the Caracciolo class.

segments.summary: France may need to cancel unsuitable designs and invest for a better answer to Italian fast battleships, while Italy has a strong case for finishing the Caracciolos and sustaining its industry.

segments.title: Caracciolos as an industrial and logistical programme
segments.body: Italy begins this scenario economically weak and in need of infrastructure investment, but it has also acquired Austrian industrial assets after the First World War. Completing the four Caracciolo hulls slowly would use equipment already purchased, provide unified employment, and preserve the capability needed for later construction. The remaining treaty allowance could support four more modern ships in the 1930s instead of expensive reconstructions of older dreadnoughts. If a Caracciolo entered service before Britain's new ships, its 28-knot combination of speed and protection could set the benchmark for the fast-battleship era. That prospect would push the Royal Navy away from slow Nelson-style successors. Italy might also keep fifteen-inch guns in the next generation because a single calibre simplifies supply and industrial support.

evidence.note: The transcript connects Caracciolo completion to purchased material, employment, Austrian industrial assets, fast-battleship competition, and gun-calibre standardization.

segments.summary: Completing the four Caracciolos could preserve employment and absorb existing material before Italy builds a second generation of fast battleships.

segments.title: Lexingtons as a US reconnaissance force
segments.body: In this version of the treaty, five Lexingtons form a reconnaissance-oriented force at the broad end of the battlecruiser spectrum. Their size, sixteen-inch guns, and speed would give the US Navy a marked advantage over the four smaller, fourteen-inch-gunned Kongos in scouting and movement. Completing USS Washington would create four Colorados, while replacing Arkansas, Wyoming, Florida, and Utah could eventually add three modern battleships. Alternatively, Washington and the unfinished America could become carriers, changing both the battle line and the development of American naval aviation. Keeping some capital-ship work alive could also reduce reliance on the enormous four-stack destroyer programme. Treaty choices therefore interact with congressional funding, existing contracts, yard activity, and the possible emergence of battlecruiser-carrier scouting groups.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Lexington roles, US capital-ship options, and possible carrier conversions.

segments.summary: Five Lexington battlecruisers would give the United States a powerful Pacific reconnaissance force, while completion or conversion choices for other hulls shape its battleship and carrier balance.

segments.title: Battlecruisers as a spectrum of fleet roles
segments.body: Battlecruisers form a spectrum rather than a single technical type. At one end are reconnaissance-oriented ships such as the Lexingtons, designed to find, screen, and move ahead of the battle fleet. Other battlecruisers are optimized to destroy their own type or reinforce the battle line as a second formation. German and Japanese designs accept more of that supporting battle-line role because those navies have fewer battleships, whereas the Royal Navy can release its battlecruisers for wider missions. Fast battleships lie farther along the spectrum, sacrificing less fighting power for speed, while conventional battleships emphasize protection and sustained punishment.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes reconnaissance battlecruisers, battlecruiser-killers, second-line ships, fast battleships, and heavily protected battleships.

segments.summary: The label battlecruiser covers reconnaissance ships, battlecruiser-killers, and second-line fleet units whose design balance depends on the navy assigning the mission.

segments.title: USS Washington and the US sixteen-inch battle line
segments.body: Completing USS Washington as the fourth Colorado would be a politically easy concession because its construction was already funded and few signatories would object. Together with the five Lexington battlecruisers, that choice initially gives the US Navy nine sixteen-inch-gun capital ships. Retiring Arkansas, Wyoming, Florida, and Utah could later release room for three modern battleships, raising the total to twelve. Britain would have fewer sixteen-inch ships but more fifteen-inch ships, so the headline tonnage ratio would still conceal different force compositions. Treaty equality can therefore produce dissimilar fleets once governments choose which existing hulls to finish or replace.

evidence.note: The transcript considers completing USS Washington, replacing four older battleships, and the resulting British-American gun-calibre balance.

segments.summary: Completing Washington and replacing four older battleships could give the United States a twelve-ship, sixteen-inch-gun core while keeping treaty tonnage nominally balanced with Britain.

segments.title: Congress, carrier conversions, and a US scouting force
segments.body: American treaty choices remain constrained by Congress and the political demand for economy, so permission to build does not guarantee that every capital ship appears. Continuing selected capital-ship contracts could keep yards active and reduce pressure to complete so many four-stack destroyers, shifting procurement effects into other categories. With most Lexington hulls retained as battlecruisers, the United States has fewer obvious carrier conversions and may initially postpone new carrier construction. America, Washington, or both could instead be converted, though each choice changes the battle line. A carrier based on one of those hulls could operate with the five Lexingtons as a reconnaissance and presence force. That experience might then encourage purpose-built carriers to support battlecruiser-carrier task groups before the Second World War.

evidence.note: The transcript links congressional restraint, destroyer contracts, possible America or Washington conversions, and Lexington-centred scouting groups.

segments.summary: Congressional restraint could delay new carriers, but converting America or Washington might pair aviation with the Lexington battlecruisers and redirect destroyer spending.

segments.title: Could a stronger Washington settlement improve London?
segments.body: Later negotiations would remain difficult, but satisfaction with the Washington settlement would create more room for trades over destroyers, carriers, cruisers, and capital ships. Britain historically exchanged heavy-cruiser for light-cruiser tonnage and also pursued restrictions on submarines. The submarine was compared to a threat that could turn the whole sea into a jungle, disrupting British plans even while Britain invested heavily in anti-submarine warfare. France and Italy's earlier exchange of battlecruiser capacity for battleship tonnage provides a model for similar bargaining. A Washington settlement seen as successful could make London a continuation of an accepted order rather than a struggle to repair a failed one. That continuity might preserve restraint even while individual categories and national priorities changed.

evidence.note: The alternate Washington settlement's implications for possible London Treaty bargaining.

segments.summary: If the Washington settlement left participants more satisfied, the London Naval Treaty might continue its bargains instead of reopening so many sources of friction.

segments.title: Fast treaty fleets leave German raiders few safe roles
segments.body: The proposed British programme alters the standard German ships would have to evade or defeat. Scharnhorst and Gneisenau historically received eleven-inch guns because larger weapons were not ready, while Germany preferred fifteen-inch weapons. In this alternate fleet environment, numerous 28-knot British battleships, modernized Queen Elizabeths, and refitted battlecruisers would deny those ships a comfortable speed advantage. Deutschland-style raiders would simultaneously face 9.2-inch cruisers and more widely available fast capital ships. An interwar treaty rule could therefore change the practical usefulness of later German designs.

evidence.note: The transcript assesses Scharnhorst and Deutschland against larger, faster alternative-treaty fleets.

segments.summary: A world with numerous 28-knot, sixteen-inch-gun British ships and heavier cruisers would make Scharnhorst- and Deutschland-style German commerce raiders far harder to justify.

segments.title: Carrier aviation under a different treaty balance
segments.body: Courageous, Glorious, and Furious remain potential British conversions, but the revised carrier allowance could favour later ships resembling the Implacable class. Such a design would combine much of Illustrious's protection with an air group closer to Ark Royal's, rather than forcing the same historical compromise between armour and aircraft capacity. Better underwater protection and earlier experience with larger carriers could also improve wartime survivability and damage-control practice. The American position is less certain because battlecruiser completion reduces the number of obvious conversion hulls, yet America or Washington could still be converted. The US Navy might then develop carriers around Lexington battlecruiser scouting formations or invest its tonnage in more viable smaller designs, reshaping naval aviation before the Second World War.

evidence.note: The transcript considers British conversions, Implacable-like carriers, and US carrier alternatives.

segments.summary: Different capital-ship allowances leave Britain able to convert its existing light battlecruisers while encouraging larger, more capable carrier designs and different American carrier choices.

segments.title: Why a Yamato-like answer becomes less attractive
segments.body: The proposal changes the benchmark against which Japan must plan: a 27-knot super-battleship can no longer comfortably outmaneuver battle lines built around 28-knot ships. Enemy sixteen-inch vessels would also be numerous enough to challenge a heavier-gunned ship through numbers and mobility. At the same time, Japan has already been permitted visible naval renewal and could later build within both capital-ship categories, reducing the political pressure to compensate for cancelled construction through an exceptional design. The scenario still expects Japanese expansion in China, and a naval treaty alone would not prevent the Second World War. Greater security could nevertheless alter Japanese policy toward Britain and the United States and reduce some of the confidence, fear, and mutual misunderstanding that shaped escalation.

evidence.note: The conclusion weighs Yamato-like designs and the broader political limits of the alternate treaty.

segments.summary: With many fast sixteen-inch-gun ships already in service and Japan able to build within the treaty, a 27-knot, eighteen-inch-gun super-battleship is a less compelling answer to the strategic problem.
